name: Jade Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, a junior lineworker with the electricity company. Most mornings I check the truck gear before Sal and I go to a fault, and I like when a house lights up again; I still need help on awkward connections.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside the truck asking of you right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Imani works at a bakery and we have two children in school. The mortgage is the first bill we protect, and we have about three months of expenses put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the software can finish forms, but somebody still has to climb the pole. I wouldn't ask anyone to trust a screen over a voltage check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still the junior who needs a second look at a tricky connection. My partner's pay from the bakery and my line wages meet the mortgage, but three months of expenses is all we've put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the morning repair rota and ask my lead to watch my terminations once a week. If the company adds a form tool, I'll use the paper checklist beside it for the first month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe when the work stays familiar. The mortgage direct debit still makes me check our account twice near payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a normal Tuesday like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At six I load cones, gloves and the tester, then ride out with Sal, my lead, to a fault or a scheduled replacement. I like seeing lights come back on, but I hate holding up the crew when I need a second explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Imani we can keep the children's swimming lessons for now. We'd still put off replacing the kitchen window because the mortgage and school shoes have first claim.

say: I'd tell my crew that **forms** may change while our repair calls and pay keep coming.
I would insist on a **voltage check** before anyone trusts a screen near live equipment.
think: My **junior standing** still makes each unfamiliar connection slow, even without major AI change.
Our **three-month cushion** feels small beside the mortgage and two children's regular costs.
do: Keep taking the **morning repair rota** and request weekly checks of my terminations.
Use a **paper checklist** beside any new form tool for its first month.
feel: I feel **relieved** about familiar work, though payday still tightens my stomach.
S0.quote: I wouldn't ask anyone to trust a screen over a voltage check.
fieldNote: She links safety to **physical checking**, reflecting the mistakes she still fears making as a junior lineworker.
Her outward confidence sits beside a **mortgage calculation** that depends on both wages continuing each month.

steps.text: Keep taking the morning repair rota and request weekly termination checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch can buy and book faster, but the field crew should sign off its own isolation. I'm not putting my hands where a planning program says it's safe without testing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work may shrink before my climbing work does, yet fewer coordinators could mean longer days for us. I'm not quick with new screens, so I'd worry the company starts judging me on entries instead of repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll ask Sal to show me the new work-order screen after our shift, one job at a time. If the rota gets thin in the first year, I'll stop the weekend takeaway and ask the neighbouring utility about openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel prickly when people call the paperwork easy. I can manage a change if someone shows me at a real job rather than handing me a login.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the work order gives you trouble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fault code and the material list sit on different pages, and I lose my place in wet gloves. Last Friday Sal caught me ordering two connectors when we needed four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might lose hours first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nina in scheduling comes to mind because she spends her day moving jobs around a screen. I don't know if her post goes, but the company might leave a vacancy open when someone quits.

say: I'd say faster **dispatch** can help, but the field crew must test and sign off its own isolation.
I would tell colleagues that **wet-glove repairs** do not look like work done from a screen.
think: My climbing may last, but **fewer coordinators** could leave the crew with longer days.
I fear being judged by **screen entries** while I'm still learning the repair work.
do: Ask Sal for **work-order practice** after shifts this winter, using one real job at a time.
Stop the **weekend takeaway** if the rota thins, then ask the neighbouring utility about openings.
feel: I feel **defensive** about paperwork and willing to learn when somebody shows me on a real call.
S1.quote: I'm not putting my hands where a planning program says it's safe without testing.
fieldNote: Her safety argument is specific: **isolation** must be checked at the job, even when planning improves elsewhere.
She sees the office changes reaching her through **longer shifts** and performance screens, despite low exposure in the field.

steps.text: Practice the new work-order screen with Sal after shifts
Stop the weekend takeaway if the repair rota thins
Ask the neighbouring utility about vacancies if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 doesn't climb our poles, though the office may change overnight. Robots arriving around 2031 would reach the line itself, and that's where I'd stop talking so boldly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 45 when the thinking system arrives and 48 when the robots arrive. The company could remove junior places first. Three months' savings won't carry four people through a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'll take every supervised fault call Sal offers and write the safe sequence in my notebook. In 2029, if the desk changes cut our hours, I'll apply to both nearby utilities; before robots arrive I'll ask the training office about paid inspection work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a jolt when I picture a machine at the top of our ladder. The children will still need school costs, and I can't make our mortgage disappear by being brave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on supervised calls now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I passed the certificate, but a live fault after rain still takes me longer than the old hands. My best case is becoming useful enough to keep while the company decides what to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would inspection work protect you after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know; a robot might do the inspection too. I'd ask whether the paid course leads to an actual vacancy before I put our mortgage money into it.

say: I'd tell the crew **thinking AI** reaches the office in 2028, while robots threaten our linework around 2031.
I would admit the **robot date** makes my usual safety argument less certain.
think: At 45, I could lose a **junior position** before my 48th birthday brings robots to field work.
Our **three months' savings** cannot cover a long job search, mortgage and two children's school costs.
do: Take **supervised fault calls** now and record the safe sequence in my notebook.
Apply to **two nearby utilities** if hours fall in 2029 and ask about paid inspection training before 2031.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about keeping four people housed if paid linework dries up.
S2.quote: Three months' savings won't carry four people through a long search.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the office's **2028 disruption** from the field crew's later robot exposure without assuming an easy escape.
Her inspection idea is **conditional** on a real vacancy and paid training, showing how little risk the mortgage permits.

steps.text: Take supervised fault calls and record safe sequences now
Apply to both nearby utilities if hours fall in 2029
Ask about paid inspection training tied to a vacancy before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our crew five years is enough to watch what fails and what actually works. Thinking AI in 2031 could clear the office desks, but a machine on the line around 2034 is the harder conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 when AGI reaches thinking work and 51 when robots can do the physical job. The children would be older, but the mortgage would still be there; I can't count on retirement at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Sal for one extra fault assessment each month and keep the sign-offs in my training folder. By 2032 I'd apply for the paid network inspection course if the utility posts a real opening, and I'd keep working the lines during its first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me room to try, and that steadies me. I'm still uneasy about learning a new role just as someone may build a robot for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course real enough for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted position, a wage while I train and a supervisor willing to say what inspection work stays human until 2034. I won't borrow against the house for a certificate with no job at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our eldest would be near leaving school and our youngest would be in the later school years. I hope the costs shift, but I won't pretend they vanish on a birthday.

say: I'd say five years gives the crew time to **watch results** before changing how we work.
I would warn that **2034 robots** could reach the line itself after thinking work changes in 2031.
think: At 51, I cannot treat **retirement** as the answer to a robot doing physical linework.
Older children may cost differently, while our **mortgage** remains and inspection might also become automated.
do: Complete **monthly fault assessments** and keep every sign-off in my training folder.
Apply for a **paid inspection course** by 2032 only if a real position is posted.
feel: I feel **steadier** with five years, yet doubtful that another certificate guarantees work.
S3.quote: I won't borrow against the house for a certificate with no job at the end.
fieldNote: The longer lead time lets her pursue **documented competence** rather than jump into unfamiliar technology at once.
She asks for **paid training and vacancies** because family obligations persist into her early fifties.

steps.text: Complete monthly fault assessments and file every sign-off
Apply for the paid inspection course if a vacancy is posted by 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade is long enough to teach the children and finish a lot of repairs properly. Thinking AI in 2036 may take the office work; robots around 2039 could still take ours, however well we trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 for the robots. The children could be working or studying by then, but I can't assume they're independent or that a pension starts before my wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the line job and pay an extra small amount on the mortgage whenever overtime comes in. By 2037 I'd ask for a place in the utility's paid safety assessor course if it still leads to work, then continue my shifts while learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less trapped because ten years gives us choices. I still hate the thought that my best years at this trade might end before I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much extra would go to the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months it would be nothing; on a good overtime month I'd put 100 toward the principal. Imani and I would decide after the bills, not promise a fixed amount we can't meet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade carefully and keep asking what the tools can do. I wouldn't tell my children power lines guarantee a lifetime of wages, because I couldn't say that honestly.

say: I'd tell colleagues a **decade** lets us work and teach the children before either AI date.
I would also say **2039 robots** may still reach our trade despite years of experience.
think: At 56, I cannot assume **pension income** will replace line wages when robots arrive.
Our children's costs may change by then, but **mortgage payments** remain until we actually clear the debt.
do: Keep my **line shifts** and put up to 100 of good-month overtime toward mortgage principal.
Ask for **paid safety assessor training** by 2037 only if it still leads to a job.
feel: I feel **less trapped** by a decade, while grieving the possible end of my trade.
S4.quote: I wouldn't tell my children power lines guarantee a lifetime of wages, because I couldn't say that honestly.
fieldNote: A longer horizon changes her response to **mortgage reduction**, but she avoids claiming a fixed payment in every month.
She accepts that **physical work** may also be automated and makes any course depend on paid employment.

steps.text: Continue line shifts through the preparation years
Pay up to 100 extra on mortgage principal after good overtime months
Ask for paid safety assessor training if jobs exist by 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there's scarcely time to become a solid lineworker before the office changes, then robots reach the field. Paid training attached to a posted job and clear notice about staffing would help more than a cheerful presentation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks a machine's work after a storm. I'd want a named person to sign off the isolation, because a family waiting for power won't care whether the mistake came from a worker or a robot.

headlineQuote: I'd want a named person to sign off the isolation, because a family waiting for power won't care whether the mistake came from a worker or a robot.
portrait: Jade is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** who loves restoring power but still asks for help on difficult connections.
Her partner's bakery wage and her own typical pay support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with three months saved.
She learns unfamiliar tools slowly, grounding her views in **physical safety checks** and supervised practice rather than promises about software.
The two-year AGI warning **alarms** her; longer warnings allow conditional paid training and modest mortgage reduction.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves Jade little time to strengthen her linework before office changes and later robots.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** tied to an actual posted job and clear staffing notice would let her plan without risking mortgage money.
